title: For the Gamblers Among Us
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note draws an analogy between compulsive gamblers and a specific type of high-energy risk-taker found in many organizations. Citing research on gambling psychology, the author argues that what drives frequent gamblers isn't winning but the excitement of the action itself — and that the same craving for arousal and adventure shows up in team members who thrive on disruption and unnecessary risk with the organization's resources. Rather than suppressing these excitement-seeking intrapreneurs, the piece argues leaders should manage them with clear parameters and frequent check-ins, since they are often the same people who generate the organization's most valuable innovations. The core leadership move described is neither restriction nor indulgence but calibrated oversight — letting risk-takers operate while keeping them from outrunning what's reasonable.
points: Frequent gamblers are driven less by winning than by the excitement of the action itself — a psychological pattern that shows up in certain high-energy team members too.
Excitement-seeking intrapreneurs are often an organization's best source of disruptive innovation, which is why leaders shouldn't simply try to shut them down.
The right move is calibrated oversight: clear parameters and frequent check-ins rather than either suppression or unchecked freedom.
Leaders who identify which colleagues are motivated primarily by action, not outcome, can protect the organization from unnecessary downside without losing their creative upside.
quotes: Most frequent gamblers are indifferent to loss. While they prefer to win, that's not the real goal behind placing bets.
The so-called "action" of gambling consumes 100 percent of a gambler's attention and creates an intensity of experience that gamblers crave.
Failure doesn't bother them nearly as much as it does others because it is equally as captivating as success.
Good leaders identify the excitement-seeking intrapreneurs who will take unnecessary chances with house money.
Checking in frequently with the risk-takers and giving them clear parameters as to what they can and cannot do serve to help everyone.
A check on reality is all a risk-taker really needs. Leaders guard the gate, while letting everyone through.
